item.title: King Charles Says U.K.’s Role in Slave Trade ‘Fills My Heart With Horror’
item.description:
King Charles III on Tuesday expressed “profound personal sorrow” and “horror” over Britain’s role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, telling leaders of the country’s former colonies that the consequences of that history still “resonate with contemporary force.”

As expected, the king did not offer a formal apology for Britain’s trafficking of millions of enslaved people from Africa in the 1700s and 1800s. As the ceremonial head of state, he is constitutionally unable to apologize on behalf of Britain unless directed to by the government.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said last week that he was open to a formal apology, in a major change of British policy.

King Charles added to his previous expressions of regret by acknowledging that slavery still casts a shadow over the nations that were once part of the British Empire.

“As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow,” Charles said in a speech in St. John’s, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, at a meeting of the Commonwealth, a voluntary organization that includes 56 nations.

The king previously said that slavery “forever stains” British history, and he asserted last week that the country should directly “acknowledge the great suffering of the past.” His remarks followed years of pressure from leaders of the Commonwealth for Britain to apologize and pay reparations.

The king’s expression of royal contrition and Mr. Burnham’s shift in the government’s longstanding position on an apology for slavery are part of a concerted effort by both leaders to keep the Commonwealth from fracturing amid growing demands that Britain face up to its history.

Formed in 1949, the group of mostly former colonies is a remnant of the once-sprawling empire and a reminder to some of how much British influence has waned in the past century. As an organization, the Commonwealth has no real power, little money to distribute and a vague mission.

“It is time to admit that the Commonwealth does not only not serve its purpose, but works against its premise of post-imperial comity,” Ben Judah, who served as a top adviser to a former British foreign secretary, wrote on social media recently. He called for a restructuring of the organization.

But for many of the small, impoverished nations in the group, it serves as a forum to connect with their larger counterparts, including Britain, India, Australia and New Zealand. For Britain, the Commonwealth provides an opportunity to counter China’s influence on trade, investment, security and the environment.

“It allows us to draw on the collective ingenuity of a third of humanity to address the challenges confronting us all,” the king said in his remarks on Tuesday. “This, it seems to me, is the vital essence of the Commonwealth.”

In recent years, those opportunities have been overshadowed by growing demands for action — not just words — to address Britain’s slaveholding history.

Those calls grew louder in the past week, as the king traveled to the Bahamas and Guyana before arriving in Antigua for the Commonwealth meeting. On Thursday, hours before Charles met with Mohamed Irfaan Ali, the president of Guyana, Mr. Ali said in an interview that an apology for slavery should be “the next step.”

Mr. Burnham, who attended the Commonwealth meeting in Antigua on Tuesday alongside King Charles, tried to preemptively address those increasingly vocal demands last week.

In an essay in The Guardian, he wrote that his government was open to a structured conversation with countries affected by the trans-Atlantic slave trade, which he called “a brutal and barbaric violation.” Mr. Burnham added: “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.”

He rejected, however, calls for reparations, saying that British people should not be “held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

In Antigua, officials said Mr. Burnham would tell other leaders of Commonwealth nations that Britain is “open to discussions about the past.”

British government officials said a formal apology could emerge after the dialogue with Commonwealth nations. The BBC reported that could be within the next year, perhaps when Britain holds the rotating presidency of the Group of 20 countries.

For Mr. Burnham, the issue is a politically tricky one back home, where he has focused the early part of his premiership on addressing the rising cost of living and the need to rebuild the country’s social safety net.

Polls suggest a majority of people are open to a discussion about an apology. But many Britons say they do not believe current government funds should be used to pay for the sins of a long-ago government at a time when their own economic fortunes are declining.

It is not clear whether Mr. Burnham’s gesture — to move toward an apology while rejecting reparations — will completely satisfy either the Commonwealth nations or his own constituents. Speaking to reporters, Mr. Burnham drew a distinction between his opposition to reparations and his support for helping the economies of struggling nations.

“I’ve been very clear that we do not support reparations,” he said. “But it’s not the case that we don’t support countries in the Commonwealth around development, and helping them with debt issues that they’ve got.”

On Tuesday, the prime minister is expected to announce an effort to help Commonwealth nations restructure their debt, allowing them to pay over a longer period and at lower interest rates. In his essay last week, he said that he had asked Gordon Brown, a former British prime minister and a long-serving chancellor of the Exchequer under Tony Blair’s premiership, to attend the meeting on Tuesday and lead the debt talks.

Mr. Burnham will also announce a task force to encourage the development of critical minerals, his office said. And he will promise that Britain will invest 40 million pounds (about $53 million) over the next three years to accelerate critical infrastructure investment in the Caribbean.

Leaders of Commonwealth nations are likely to welcome those announcements. But they fall short of the ongoing demands from some countries that Britain make monetary compensation to the descendants of enslaved people.

Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said on Saturday that Mr. Burnham’s openness to an apology was welcomed. But she did not back away from demands for reparations.

“On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she wrote in a statement.

After addressing the slavery issue, King Charles focused most of his Tuesday speech on opportunities and challenges for the Commonwealth nations.

“What unites this extraordinary and unique group of countries even more deeply is our values,” the king said. “Of democracy and the rule of law; of respect, equal dignity and human rights; of sustainable development; of peace and security. These values have never been more important, contested as they are on so many fronts.”

The king did not shy away from acknowledging the turmoil across the world.

“All around us, trust between nations is under critical strain, as international norms and systems are tested to their limits,” he said. “Brutal conflict stalks our world, destroying lives and casting long shadows across the globe.”

But he also expressed optimism about the future, noting a nature initiative intended to help protect biodiversity and increase conservation. He talked about plans for an insurance mechanism to help countries become more climate-resilient and to deal with natural disasters. And he endorsed efforts to bring heads of governments, investors and business leaders together to increase development in small economies.

item.title: America’s Arab Allies Brace for War as Trump’s Midterm Deadline Looms
item.description:
In the marble-floored atria of a five-star hotel in Manama, Bahrain’s capital, military officers in full regalia mingled with ambassadors and political analysts last weekend, swapping business cards and chatting over plates of tiramisù infused with Arabic coffee.

The smiles and the warm handshakes at the gathering — the Manama Dialogue, an annual security conference — belied the grim topic underpinning much of the conversation. The possibility that the United States might, within days, reignite its war with Iran, prompting a barrage of Iranian missiles and drones on the very city where they were meeting, hung over the event like a dark cloud.

As President Trump weighs a renewed attack on Iran sometime after the midterm elections on Tuesday, Gulf Arab officials fear that their countries — which host American military bases, Western companies and valuable oil and gas facilities — will be the hardest hit, as they were after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February. They also fear that the fighting will be worse this time around.

The Iranian and American positions on a potential deal to stave off a crisis are still “far apart,” Anwar Gargash, a senior official from the United Arab Emirates, told the conference audience. “If these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.”

The U.S. military carried out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Monday, according to U.S. officials. Still, Mr. Trump told Fox News on the same day that “there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”

American and Israeli military officials have drawn up an expanded list of targets to strike, including energy infrastructure and other sites vital to the Iranian economy. Iran has warned that it would retaliate fiercely, targeting critical infrastructure and underwater communications cables in the region.

The Gulf countries are already bruised, working to repair energy infrastructure and radar systems that were damaged in the last round of attacks and coping with major economic disruptions. And while their governments operate advanced air defense systems and have worked to harden their defenses, they are constrained in their ability to fend off attacks by a global shortage of missile interceptors.

Saudi Arabia is also preparing for the possibility of a war on several fronts, as the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen fire near-daily volleys of missiles and drones at the kingdom, targeting airports and oil facilities.

The energy-rich Gulf countries have long marketed themselves to tourists and investors as safe havens in a volatile Middle East. Now, some citizens and residents are stockpiling water and cash, or preparing “go bags” full of emergency essentials to grab if they need to flee their homes. Others have changed their travel plans to return home as soon as possible, worried that they could be stuck outside the region if missile and drone attacks force countries to close their airspace.

While a preliminary cease-fire was reached in June — followed by several months of limbo and intermittent bursts of fighting — people in the Gulf fear that it is now “just a matter of time” before their countries get dragged back into a full-blown war, said Khalid Al-Jaber, executive director of the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, a research institute in Qatar.

“The scary part this time is that the war is going to be worse than before,” he said. “It’s going to be bigger. It’s going to be much harder for everyone.”

The past few days have been marked by a flurry of diplomacy and calls for de-escalation among President Trump’s closest Arab allies, including Saudi Arabia, which sent its defense minister to Iran last week to make the case for peace. Qatar has been leading an effort to reach a deal between Iranian and U.S. officials before it is too late, and in recent days Iranian officials have signaled that those negotiations have made some progress.

While Mr. Trump has said he would not attack before the midterm elections, he has hinted that all bets are off after that.

As a result, the elections have become a grim marker of time for people across the Gulf Arab states, many of whom know little about the American electoral system or the candidates running for office.

Instead, they know that before the midterms are over, they can reasonably expect their lives to continue as normal. They can drive to work and go to the mall, peruse Netflix on their phones and tend to their gardens with plentiful desalinated water.

After then, nobody knows what will happen.

“We are extremely worried,” Badr Abdelatty, Egypt’s foreign minister, said at the conference in Manama. “We have to push very hard in order to prevent the escalation. We are very confident that the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere.”

Donald Blome, the U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs, told the audience at the conference that diplomatic channels between the United States and Iran were still active, even as the United States was “prepared to go in another direction.”

The event ended on Sunday, after which many of the attendees departed the region as quickly as possible.

Ismaeel Naar contributed reporting from Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

item.title: Bomb Threats Disrupt Several Flights Across Europe
item.description:
Bomb threats targeted at least 7 planes in Europe on Tuesday, briefly disrupting flights as the local authorities carried out security checks at several airports.

All of the planes landed safely, and officials said that no explosives had been found. It was not immediately clear who had made the threats, how they were issued or whether there was any connection between them. The threats came a day after a midair bomb scare forced a plane leaving London to make an emergency landing in Budapest.

Anxiety over airspace security is high in Europe, where a spate of hybrid warfare attacks and intimidation tactics have rattled air travel in recent months as Russia’s war against Ukraine spills over its borders. Last month, an airport in Germany briefly shut down after a false alarm about a possible hijacking on an incoming flight from Greece.

Here are where the threats were reported.

Polish officials responded to “an alarm regarding a bomb threat on board” a plane traveling from London just before 10 a.m. on Tuesday, Warsaw Modlin Airport said in a statement on social media.

The plane landed minutes later at Modlin, which mostly serves budget airlines and is northwest of the capital, instead of the larger Warsaw Chopin Airport, its intended destination, the statement said.

Officials and pyrotechnic teams met the plane, which was carrying 181 people, and Modlin temporarily ceased operations. After noon, the bomb alert was “canceled,” the airport said.

A flight traveling from Copenhagen to Warsaw and operated by the Scandinavian airline SAS was also targeted by a threat, according to the airline.

The aircraft landed normally and the passengers disembarked, Alexandra Lindgren Kaoukji, a spokeswoman for SAS, said in an email. She said the police in Warsaw were now handling the matter.

In response to a bomb threat, the police in the southern city of Murcia inspected a plane that had traveled from Manchester, England but “ruled out the presence of explosives on the plane,” said Francisco Lucas, a local Spanish official. There were 114 passengers and seven crew members on board.

Mr. Lucas said on social media that Murcia’s international airport had resumed normal operations after the threat.

The Bulgarian transportation ministry said that two planes targeted by bomb threats landed in Sofia, the capital, on Tuesday, but that officials found no explosive devices on board.

One plane was a Wizz Air flight coming from Italy, while the other was a Ryanair flight from Dublin, the ministry said in a statement.

Two Ryanair flights arriving at Fiumicino Airport in Rome were disrupted by bomb scares, the airport press office said in an email. One came from Lisbon and the other flew in from Dublin.

The Roman airport authorities said that there had been “an anonymous report of a suspected bomb on board” the flight coming from Lisbon. Police bomb disposal experts assessed the situation, and the alert was lifted.

The flight from Dublin was escorted to the airport by the Italian Air Force, the airport said. After security checks, no explosives were found.

There were about 300 people on board the two flights, including passengers and crew, the airport said. “The relevant authorities are investigating the origin of the threats,” it said.

item.title: On Cusp of Renewed War, More Iranians Are Calling for Nuclear Weapons
item.description:
From pulpits at Friday prayers to street rallies, Iranian clerics and officials are increasingly urging the country’s leaders to reverse their longtime pledge not to pursue nuclear weapons.

This demand, once seen as a fringe position held by hard-liners, is moving into mainstream public debate, and the shift could have dramatic consequences for Iran, whose government has for decades argued that its nuclear program was solely for peaceful purposes.

“We must be equipped with nuclear weapons — so that we can fight the criminal America with strength, God willing,” Ali Sepahvand, the Friday prayer leader in Iran’s western city of Kuhdasht, said last week, according to a widely distributed video.

As his voice echoed through a prayer hall, covered in photographs of commanders killed in the war with the United States and Israel this past year, the congregants chanted: “Nuclear deterrence is our inalienable right!”

The growing calls for Iran to pursue nuclear weapons come as the country’s leaders engage in diplomatic efforts to stave off renewed war with the United States and Israel, an outcome widely considered likely after the American midterm elections on Tuesday.

For decades, Iran’s officials have publicly endorsed the fatwa, or religious edict, from its supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, which forbade the development and use of nuclear weapons. Issued in his capacity as the head of Iran’s theocratic state, his decree barred Iranian institutions, including the military and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, from pursuing a nuclear bomb.

Yet at the same time, Western intelligence agencies in past years reported signs Iran was enriching uranium to levels close to those that could be used to develop a bomb. Some officials in Israel and the United States accused Iran of preparing to build one, regardless of the fatwa.

To curb this threat, the United States and other world powers reached an agreement with Iran in 2015 to restrict its nuclear activities. Three years later, President Trump pulled out of that agreement.

Ayatollah Khamenei’s strategy, regional analysts say, had been to keep Iran’s nuclear intentions ambiguous in hopes of deterring attacks on Iran without it actually becoming a nuclear power.

But that approach failed to prevent the two wars Israel and the United States have waged against Iran since June 2025 — including the one in which Mr. Khamenei was himself killed in February.

“He created this neither in nor out situation, where they paid for a bomb they didn’t have,” said Mohammad Ali Shabani, an Iran analyst who edits the independent regional news site Amwaj.media. “Now, there is this sense that unless you have this ultimate weapon, you could end up at the mercy of not just the U.S., but Israel, at any point.”

President Trump’s own comments may strengthen this assessment, analysts say.

“If they had a nuclear weapon, I’d be calling the Supreme Leader and I’d be saying, ‘Mr. Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’ As opposed to bombing the crap out of him,” Mr. Trump said at the Republican midterm convention in September.

Inside Iran, calls for withdrawing from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, or N.P.T., which prohibits development of a nuclear weapon, have been growing ever since Israel and the United States attacked in 2025.

In recent weeks, an increasing number of Iranian political and religious figures have added their voices to this chorus, suggesting to some Iran analysts that there is an effort orchestrated, or at least enabled, by the country’s leadership.

It is unclear whether serious debate over Iran’s nuclear doctrine has reached the new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei. But on Saturday, Iran’s top national security figure, Mohsen Rezaei, said in an interview on state television that Iran’s leaders were discussing it.

“No new decision has been made yet,” he said. “Of course, the debate now is whether we want to keep the same doctrine we had before the war, if war breaks out again.”

Advocating for withdrawal from the N.P.T. was once a minority position within Iran’s leadership, said Mohammad Ghaderi, a foreign affairs expert in Tehran.

Now, he argued, it is becoming a majority view. “They argue that if the military threats from the United States and Israel persist, withdrawing from the N.P.T. represents a crucial step toward establishing deterrence,” he said.

Raising the nuclear prospect at a time when Iran could be at the cusp of another possible attack by the United States or Israel may itself be a strategy, said Omid Memarian, an Iran analyst at DAWN, a Washington-based Middle East research group.

Mr. Rezaei’s entry into the debate, while Qatar has been leading intensive mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran, may be an attempt to push the United States to reach a deal, Mr. Memarian said.

“They are playing with this card: If the negotiation fails, we will seek a different path, and it will be costly for you,” he said.

Especially notable has been the number of Friday prayer leaders adding their voices to the calls and effectively challenging the late ayatollah’s fatwa.

“The taboo is gone,” said Mr. Shabani. “A religious foundation for the shift is here. The question is whether a strategic or political shift will follow.”

Some of Iran’s leading reformist figures, like the president Masoud Pezeshkian and former president Hassan Rouhani, continue to back Iran’s peaceful nuclear doctrine.

In Iran’s leading reformist newspaper, Shargh, a former diplomat, Kourosh Ahmadi, warned this week that abandoning that doctrine poses grave risks. The plethora of pro-weapon statements from prominent figures, he said, “is dangerous because it makes the work of officials trying to prevent another war more difficult.”

And until Iran could manage to build a bomb, he argued, the chances of being attacked would actually increase.

After U.S. and Israeli strikes wiped out most of Iran’s top leadership and battered its infrastructure, it is harder for critics of the nuclear option to make their case, said Sina Toossi, an Iran expert at the Center for International Policy, a Washington-based think tank.

“The central problem for advocates of restraint is explaining what Iran gained from remaining below the nuclear threshold,” he said.

At the same time, he said, a new round of U.S. attacks “could strengthen the very arguments for the nuclear weapons that Washington says it wants to prevent.”

At public prayers in Tehran on Friday, the prayer leader, Mohammad Javad Haj Ali Akbari, declared that changing Iran’s nuclear doctrine was “a national demand,” according to a video posted on social media.

His congregants immediately responded with a refrain common at government-sponsored rallies from decades past: “Nuclear energy is our inalienable right!”

“This is an old slogan,” he told them, and smiled: “We have gone way beyond that.”

Leily Nikounazar and Sanam Mahoozi contributed reporting

item.title: This Grandma Believes She Can Fix Africa’s Richest City
item.description:
To the beat of a Zulu rap song, the polished, 1990s-era BMW convertible rolled into the political rally in Johannesburg, greeted by delirious cheers from hundreds of South Africans. The car, known as a “gusheshe,” became synonymous with the hip culture that emerged from the largely impoverished townships where Black people were forced to live under apartheid.

But sitting atop the gusheshe (pronounced GOO-shay-shay) was someone South Africans may hardly associate with Black culture. It was Helen Zille, 75, a white grandmother who has been criticized for her stances on race, including past statements suggesting that colonialism had its benefits, denouncing affirmative action in South Africa and embracing American right-wing terms like “wokeness.”

Yet, as she campaigns to lead South Africa’s largest city, Johannesburg, ahead of Wednesday’s election, Ms. Zille is betting that race no longer guides many South Africans’ decisions in the voting booth.

Instead, she argues, South Africans are more concerned with quality-of-life issues like water shortages, crumbling roads and public safety. And her blunt, rugged style, she says, is best suited to getting Africa’s wealthiest city working again.

With an outsize persona and social media outreach that feels more Gen Z than baby boomer, Ms. Zille has injected excitement, and some controversy, into the typically bland, predictable ritual of South African electioneering.

“Lots of people don’t like me,” Ms. Zille, the mayoral candidate for the Democratic Alliance, or D.A., said in an interview. “It’s fine. You don’t even have to like the D.A. You just have to love Johannesburg to consolidate your vote behind us.”

Ms. Zille’s strategy has put her ahead in the polls in Johannesburg, the biggest prize in an election in which millions of voters are expected to choose mayors and city councilors across the nation. The local elections could have important repercussions for the national political landscape, analysts said.

The African National Congress, the party of Nelson Mandela that led South Africa out of apartheid, has experienced a sharp electoral decline. In the country’s past two major elections, less than half of South Africa’s voters chose the A.N.C., an unheard-of development for the party since it came to power after apartheid ended in 1994.

Polls and analysts suggest an even further slide is coming this election, with the A.N.C. projected to be surpassed as the largest party in most of South Africa’s eight major metropolitan cities. (It’s currently the largest in six of them.) The A.N.C.’s diminution could deepen fighting within the party, experts say, and intensify tensions in the national government coalition led by the A.N.C. The party could also be forced to moderate its policy ambitions and accede to some of its rivals’ demands.

Most metro areas in South Africa are not projected to have clear-cut winners in the election, raising fears among some analysts that parties will form unstable governing coalitions that will make life harder for ordinary South Africans.

“I’m really pessimistic about the future of this country,” said Bheki Mngomezulu, a political science professor at Nelson Mandela University.

Historically, the A.N.C. had not announced mayoral candidates before elections, instead relying on its brand to attract voters. This year, with Ms. Zille’s popularity presenting a possible threat, the A.N.C. broke with tradition and announced three finalists for its mayoral candidate in Johannesburg, a sprawling city of nearly five million people.

But the party bungled that effort when its leadership failed to formally submit the name of one of those finalists, Frank Chikane, to the electoral commission. That means he is currently not eligible to become mayor.

The A.N.C. has turned to Cyril Ramaphosa, South Africa’s president and the party’s leader, in an effort to defy the grim projections about how it will fare in the elections. He is the party’s most respected figure.

Mr. Ramaphosa has been barnstorming the country trying to persuade voters to stick with the party. Last month, he waded through crowds in the township of Soweto, speaking with voters complaining that they lacked water, electricity and jobs.

“When you do the balance, when you look at the balance sheet, there’s more positive than negative,” Mr. Ramaphosa told a crowd gathered on the street, referring to the A.N.C.’s governing record.

In South Africa, voters select parties that then form coalitions to pick the mayor. About 80 parties are competing in Johannesburg. But Ms. Zille is polling way ahead of other candidates, though still less than the 50 percent needed to become mayor outright.

Her campaign has been hyper-focused on making the A.N.C.’s governing failures go viral.

She has posted to social media videos of her “snorkeling” in a huge pothole filled with water from a burst pipe; paddling an inflatable boat in flooded Soweto streets; and directing traffic at a broken traffic light. She conducted an unannounced “oversight” visit to a crumbling, abandoned municipal building, unveiling a dramatic video that included being chased by security guards.

Shortly before the political rally last month in which she rode on the back of the convertible, she posted a video of herself screeching a gusheshe in circles, kicking up smoke and leaving skid marks. Spinning cars is a popular activity in South African townships.

“Other parties will spin you stories,” she said into the camera. “We’ll spin into action.”

The comments section lit up with laughing emojis, clapping hands, flames and praise for “Gogo Helen.” (Gogo is the term used for grandmother in Black communities.)

“You know what, take my vote,” one commenter wrote.

Critics, though, have accused Ms. Zille of pandering to Black communities by reaching for caricatures and stereotypes. Some have called her stunts gimmicks that avoid the hard work of engaging Black voters.

And Dada Morero, the current mayor of Johannesburg and a member of the A.N.C., has criticized the D.A. for fomenting inequalities in the cities it has governed and cast doubt on Ms. Zille’s commitment to Johannesburg.

“This sudden interest in Johannesburg by the D.A. is not about residents; it is about politics,” he told a South African news outlet in response to one of Ms. Zille’s viral social media posts.

Most public polls have Ms. Zille shy of 40 percent of the vote, a tally that may make it difficult for her to pull together a coalition of parties to become Johannesburg’s next mayor. But some analysts say her path to office could run through a coalition with the A.N.C., which the D.A. is already partnering with in the national government.

Before entering political office in the late 1990s, Ms. Zille was a journalist for a newspaper that was critical of the apartheid regime. She famously debunked the apartheid government’s claim that the activist Steve Biko had died from the effects of a hunger strike. Her investigation found that he had sustained extensive brain damage and bruising, suggesting that he had been killed in police custody.

In 2007, Ms. Zille became the mayor of Cape Town, South Africa’s second-largest city, and she later served a decade as the premier of Western Cape Province. It seemed as if Ms. Zille’s political career was approaching its twilight last year, when, as a top D.A. official, she was tasked with leading the party’s selection of a Johannesburg mayoral candidate.

She surveyed the field, she said, and thought about her own experience in cutthroat municipal politics.

“People get killed here, and you are always being attacked and then your name gets dragged through the mud on social media and in mainstream media,” she said. “So it’s not a job that many people want.”

Ms. Zille found that the party “didn’t have anyone who could quite rise to that,” she said.

It struck her, she said, that as a woman whose aunt lived to 104 and whose mother smoked but made it to 95, she had a lot left to give.

So she threw her hat into the ring.

item.title: Israel’s President Holds Crucial Cards in Breaking Post-Election Deadlock
item.description:
For five years, Isaac Herzog has tried to avoid controversy and heal rifts in his largely ceremonial role as the president of Israel. Now, following last week’s inconclusive election, he must make a decision that is likely to roil one half or the other of a fractured country.

One of the president’s few powers is the ability to grant a party leader the mandate to try and form a government. Typically, this is assigned to the head of the party that has won the most votes or appears to have the best chance of building a coalition that would command a majority in Parliament. But the law is vague, giving the president a lot of leeway over the process.

Mr. Herzog, the scion of an illustrious Israeli family who is expected to remain involved in the backroom talks throughout the process, will have to draw on his skills as a savvy negotiator and mediator — expertise he honed over his years as a lawyer and politician, including as leader of the center-left Labor party.

After working in law, he served as a government secretary under Prime Minister Ehud Barak and as a minister in multiple governments. He ran a credible but unsuccessful campaign to replace Mr. Netanyahu in the 2015 election and went on to lead the Jewish Agency, an organization that serves as a bridge between Israel and the Jewish diaspora.

A longtime advocate of national unity, he will most likely work to enable as broad a government as possible, analysts say, to try to get Israel out of what many call the political “plonter,” a Yiddish word to describe a mess, like an intricate knot that is hard to unravel.

“This is his big moment,” Nachman Shai, a former Labor minister and lawmaker, said of Mr. Herzog. “He is a polished, creative politician,” he added. “Not everyone will like his ideas, but I’m sure he will be looking for solutions to build a coalition that are out of the box.”

Starting on Wednesday, representatives of the 11 political parties elected to the new Parliament will troop through the presidential residence in a leafy neighborhood of Jerusalem to consult with Mr. Herzog and to recommend their candidate for the premiership.

Most party leaders are expected to back either Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the longtime right-wing leader, or his main center-right rival, Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief.

Note: Parties must win at least 3.25 percent of the national vote to enter the 120-seat Knesset.

Source: Israel’s Central Elections Committee

Neither man’s political bloc won an outright majority of 61 seats in the 120-member Parliament. Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud took 27 seats, making it the largest party, but his hard-right, religious coalition’s tally fell to 53 seats.

Mr. Eisenkot’s main bloc of Jewish opposition parties secured 48 seats. If the Arab-led parties that oppose Mr. Netanyahu and won 19 seats also recommend him to Mr. Herzog, the president may well grant him the first opportunity to try and form a government. Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s Jewish allies, however, have balked at the idea of a government relying on Arab support.

Mr. Herzog cannot take political sides and must remain a unifying figurehead above the fray. He has called for a “stable” government without specifying how it should be formed and has called on the parties’ representatives to consult with him with open minds and hearts.

The law allows the assigned candidate 28 days to try to form a government, though the president can extend that period by up to 14 days. If the first attempt fails, the president can give another candidate a chance or refer the efforts to Parliament. If no party leader is able to form a governing coalition, new elections would be held — an outcome that Mr. Herzog has urged them to avoid.

The kind of broad unity government that Mr. Herzog may envisage would likely require some kind of power-sharing deal between Mr. Netanyahu and Mr. Eisenkot — a prospect that faces huge obstacles.

Mr. Eisenkot says that Mr. Netanyahu must be replaced and has ruled out serving under him. Mr. Netanyahu, who has been on trial for six years following corruption charges in three separate but interlocking cases, cannot serve in a government as a minister. According to Israeli law, only a prime minister can serve under indictment.

Mr. Herzog has a potentially valuable, if highly contentious, card to play to try to bring Mr. Netanyahu on side with a unifying coalition, analysts say.

The president has the authority to issue pardons, generally for people already convicted of crimes. Mr. Netanyahu, who has denied any wrongdoing, submitted a pre-emptive request for a pardon during his trial a year ago.

Mr. Herzog has instead offered to try to initiate a mediation process to reach a plea deal and invited the attorney general and Mr. Netanyahu’s lawyer for talks. Mr. Netanyahu’s team never replied.

“A pardon can be part of a package deal,” Mr. Shai said. “It could be a way for Mr. Herzog to come to a compromise with him. Everyone is tired of the trial by now, and nobody knows how it will end.”

“Herzog is energetic, super active, primed for action,” he said. “People forget he is one of the most experienced people around,” he added.

Mitchell Barak, an analyst who worked as an aide to Mr. Netanyahu and later for President Shimon Peres, a former Labor leader, said Mr. Herzog’s history with the prime minister and the “ace” of a potential pardon could be viewed either as a conflict of interest in negotiations or as an advantage.

“He is holding a get-out-of-jail-free card for Netanyahu,” Mr. Barak added. “Or you could call it leverage,” he added.

The president’s office dismissed suggestions of a conflict of interest, saying the pardon and the efforts toward forming a government were two different tracks based on separate laws.

As president, Mr. Herzog oversaw negotiations that tried, and failed, to reach a compromise over the Netanyahu government’s plans for a judicial overhaul that caused turmoil in Israel. Mr. Shai said many Israelis had expected Mr. Herzog to take a stronger stand against the government’s moves and that the episode harmed his public standing.

Mr. Herzog also appears to have tried to build confidence on both sides of Israel’s political divide.

He has spoken out against what he called “a terrible process of brutalization” creeping into Israeli society, citing a surge of “mob” violence by Jews against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and the abuse of detainees in Israeli custody.

Mr. Herzog also recently expunged the criminal record of Elor Azaria, a former soldier who fatally shot a severely wounded Palestinian man at close range while he lay on the ground a decade ago. The man had earlier been seriously injured after he attacked an Israeli checkpoint. The president’s move baffled and angered many liberal Israelis but fulfilled a long-sought demand from Israel’s right.

Mr. Herzog also has his family legacy and reputation to consider. His grandfather, Rabbi Dr. Yitzhak Isaac Halevi Herzog, was the first Chief Rabbi of the state of Israel. His father, Chaim Herzog, served as the sixth president of Israel.

After the 1984 election, when Mr. Peres and Yitzhak Shamir, then the Likud leader, were in a deadlock, Mr. Herzog’s father played an active role in promoting the formation of a unity government, resolving the political impasse.

Mr. Herzog “is part of the country’s old guard and political elite with a storied tradition of excellence,” said Mr. Barak. “There’s a certain responsibility that comes with that.”

item.title: Why Doctors in Thailand Fear KFC
item.description:
Thanat Tantinam, a colorectal surgeon in Thailand, knows a lot of things from his medical training, like the ins and outs of the human digestive system, or bowel cancer rates. But also: Never eat Kentucky Fried Chicken at work.

Since he was a medical student, around a decade ago, the American fast food franchise has been the subject of an odd superstition among Thai doctors, many of whom believe that eating its chicken at work will lead to intolerably busy shifts.

“It’s a serious superstition in some hospitals,” said Dr. Thanat, 35. “Your colleagues might be mad if you bring KFC.”

He recently tested this theory. Between 2023 and 2024, he and several co-workers at Phatthalung Hospital in southern Thailand, his employer at the time, conducted a randomized control trial of 345 surgical shifts, comparing metrics like case load or estimated blood loss in patients from three groups of surgeons: a group that ate KFC, another that got food from a local brand named Five Star Chicken, and one that ate nothing.

The study, which was published earlier this year in the Annals of Surgery Open, a medical journal based in Philadelphia, found that eating KFC does not, in fact, lead to more work. But it also left many questions unanswered: Where did the KFC curse come from? And how had it gripped some of the most educated scientific minds in the country, including Dr. Thanat himself?

“Yes, I still believe it — maybe 80 percent out of 100,” he said. “If someone brought me KFC at work, I would keep it until past my shift.”

Such superstitions abound in Thailand, where Buddhism has blended with a mélange of other spiritual traditions like animism, Hindu rituals and Chinese astrology to create a strong affinity for the supernatural in contemporary life.

“In Thailand, superstition isn’t the opposite of modernity — it lives comfortably alongside it,” said Theeranuch Pusaksrikit, a business school professor at Chulalongkorn University who researches how superstitions affect consumerist behavior. “The same person can hold a science degree, consult an auspicious date before signing a contract and wear an amulet to work.”

No occasion is too big or too small for a sprinkle of superstition. There are the infamous black magic rituals that occasionally surface in politics, and popular customs like dressing in lucky colors corresponding to each day of the week. Last year, when a sinkhole opened up and stranded a pickup truck near Bangkok’s Vajira Hospital, Dr. Thanat’s current employer, people rushed to buy lottery tickets matching the vehicle’s license plate number.

“Each hospital has their own superstition culture,” Dr. Thanat said. He has also heard of colleagues avoiding nuts, pizza or coffee while at work, and knows of at least one hospital where bananas — otherwise regarded as a lucky food — are taboo.

But few medical superstitions have been as universal and long-running as the KFC curse, a fact that has been a point of fascination at KFC itself.

“We dug into the data, it was pretty clear,” said Suhayl Limbada, who was until recently the chief marketing officer of KFC Thailand. “There was a noticeable trend at restaurants around hospitals, there was a dip in sales.”

Two years ago, he parlayed the curse into a marketing campaign. Though riffing on cultural practices had gotten Mr. Limbada in trouble before — the fried chicken-scented incense sticks the company released for Lunar New Year were widely panned — this one was much more warmly received.

Launched on doctor’s day in November 2024, the campaign offered a kind of cleansing ritual: Chicken was sold in packaging labeled with slogans like “This is not KFC” in stores near hospitals.

Mr. Limbada has his own ideas about how the curse came to be. KFC opened in Thailand in 1984 and has since become one of the most ubiquitous fast food franchises in the country — and a trailblazer of late night delivery. It operates around 1,300 stores, far outnumbering McDonald’s, which has around 240. In even the smallest rural town, chances are there is at least a KFC.

He thinks one of these rural locations might have been the ground zero, delivering one late night to an understaffed local hospital where a hungry doctor, unaware that they were about to be hit with a sanity-shattering deluge of patients, was waiting.

The superstition has since racked up a catalog of very specific lore.

It is widely understood, for example, that it only applies to departments that cannot easily leave the hospital for meals, like surgery or emergency rooms, said Titaporn Nasaarn, a 34-year-old ER doctor at Kamalasai Hospital in northeastern Thailand.

She recalled how her colleagues once successfully co-opted the superstition for good. It was during an unusually quiet evening in the surgical intensive care unit, and some of the nurses, who wanted to work, were worried they were going to lose their upcoming shifts.

“The attending anesthesiologist performed a ritual to summon cases by ordering KFC and ordering pizza,” she said. The beds filled up. But “normally, hardly anyone dares to order it,” she added.

To everyone else, of course, KFC, with Thai spinoffs like Green Curry Chicken Rice, remains a desirable food. And at many hospitals, patients or their families occasionally treat their medical caretakers to the stuff, a gesture that invariably puts Jaruda Mamuangbon, a 42-year-old nurse at Vajira Hospital, on edge.

But she and her colleagues have noticed that the number of KFC gifts has plummeted in the last two or so years.

“We have always graciously accepted the kind gift,” Ms. Jaruda said. “But I think the patients’ families have probably picked up on the superstition from social media.”

Ms. Theeranuch, the professor, sees the widespread belief in the jinx not as a posture of anti-science, but a way for Thailand’s medical workers to keep their spirits up.

“Hospital work is intensely unpredictable, and a shared rule like ‘don’t eat KFC on shift’ may give staff a small sense of control over something inherently unpredictable,” she said. “They also build solidarity.”

Dr. Thanat has settled into a similar view. Underneath the supernatural dress of the KFC curse are, he said, more sobering earthbound realities.

It is telling that the curse has largely been confined to the country’s public hospitals, where doctors — overworked and underpaid compared with their private sector counterparts — have long called for better working conditions.

“If you work at a private hospital, you would want more patients to come,” Dr. Thanat said, adding that doctors’ compensation at private hospitals scales with greater caseloads.

“I think the KFC curse is a projection of fear,” he said. “We need a scapegoat.”

Phuriphat Dejsuphong contributed reporting.

item.title: Countries Weigh, and Worry About, What Trump Will Do After Midterm Defeat
item.description:
For two years, the world has weathered President Trump’s domineering unilateralism, enduring up-and-down tariffs, a war with Iran, aggression in Latin America, abrupt reversals on Ukraine, and a fusillade of demands for allies including Canada, Germany and Japan.

Now, with Democrats having taken control of Congress as nearly all of Mr. Trump’s preferred Republicans fall to defeat, many countries are debating what to expect from yet another case of American political whiplash.

Some analysts suggest a new Congress might slow President Trump’s most impulsive urges. Online, there was some obvious celebration. On Weibo, China’s dominant social media platform, the hashtag “Trump suffered a complete and utter defeat” was trending as results were announced.

But because presidents have enormous leeway with foreign policy, one persistent question emerged from Asia to Europe: Will the electoral losses at home spur Mr. Trump toward even more aggressive actions around the globe?

“In response to a Democrat-controlled Congress,” said Ja-Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, “Trump could try to find distractions elsewhere, including on tariffs and the use of force.”

Countries around the world are assessing how the American elections results might affect the most pressing issues in international affairs.

In Asia, which is heavily reliant on energy from the Middle East, the Democratic victory initially produced a wisp of optimism.

“In Southeast Asia, the main challenge has been inflationary pressure caused by the war in Iran. That’s made everything a lot more expensive,” Mr. Chong said. “Now there’s hope for some sort of reprieve.”

And yet, he and many others doubt that notion. Many countries have expressed concern that the war with Iran would continue escalating in the short-term — perhaps with Mr. Trump striking Iran again after the elections — worsening the squeeze on oil and gas supplies.

For now, the mood remains more grim than gleeful: Oil prices are expected to stay high for the foreseeable future, challenging businesses and leaving many to wonder what Mr. Trump might do next.

U.S. trade investigators have spent months probing more than a dozen countries accused of labor violations and overproducing everything from chemicals to cars. Now that the White House is no longer concerned about drawing attention to inflation before the elections, countries might expect a reinvigorated push to impose tariffs.

Japan, China and Vietnam are all likely targets for additional tariffs. In many countries, new levies would come on top of existing ones, lifting rates back toward where they were before the Supreme Court struck down earlier tariffs in February.

Mr. Trump still has sweeping powers over trade. Congress, however, could use its newfound leverage over the federal budget and its oversight authority to shape some of the details.

“You might see Congress pushing for more tariff carve outs and exceptions in categories that affect their constituent’s pocket books,” said Stephen Olson, a former U.S. trade negotiator and visiting fellow at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.

Generally, in Asia and elsewhere, many expect American protectionism to keep marching on, with a president seeking to leave a legacy and still determined to bend the global economy toward his views.

“People are deeply uneasy about the Trump administration’s past actions and remain anxious about the future,” said Kazuhiro Maeshima, a professor of American politics and diplomacy at Sophia University in Tokyo, discussing the mood in Japan. “While there is a hope for change, whether that change will actually materialize is unknown.”

The American elections were not expected to alter the direction of U.S.-China relations, especially regarding their on-again, off-again trade truce. Both political parties have increasingly agreed to take a tougher posture on China when it comes to economic competition and disputes over contested territory.

But on Weibo, a leading Chinese social media platform, the early results led to some initial gloating at President Trump’s expense.Xu Shaolin, a prominent commentator with nearly 4 million followers, wrote that if the losses held in both houses of Congress “this unreliable president who talks big, but is prone to making empty promises, will likely become a lame duck.”

Shi Yinhong, a professor of international relations at Renmin University in Beijing, predicted nonetheless that the Democrats’ success would mean trouble for relations between the United States and China.

Xi Jinping, China’s leader, and President Trump reached an understanding at a summit in May in favor of what China defines as “constructive, strategic stability.” But Mr. Shi predicted that this understanding would break down “because Trump suddenly becomes far from all-powerful.”

A Democratic Congress might also strengthen America’s relations with traditional United States allies, including Japan, which he said would also not be good for China.

For Taiwan, the election results could be a “potentially positive sign,” according to William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group in Taipei.

He said he thought a Democrat-led Congress might intensify its pressure on the White House to approve a long-delayed $14 billion arms package that would be a boost to Taiwan’s defenses against Chinese military threats.

Mr. Trump has threatened his country’s own partners and allies with everything from tariffs to bombs. And in some of the once-friendly nations that Mr. Trump has alienated, the public reaction veered toward relief or celebration of the Democratic wins on Tuesday.

Ryan Cox, a philosophy lecturer at the University of Sydney, said Wednesday that he was hoping to see the Democrats “slow down the power of Trump,” to accelerate “the end of the Trump era.”

Luka Leveque, a Japanese university student in Tokyo, said he was hoping “for greater consistency — both in the approach taken between our two nations and in the continuity of U.S. policy over time.”

And yet, with two years of the Trump administration to go, skepticism about his transactional leadership style and reliability remains deeply entrenched. In a recent poll of 34 countries published by the Rockefeller Foundation, just 39 percent of respondents said they were comfortable with the United States leading on the world stage.

As Max Yoeli, a senior research fellow at Chatham House in London, noted just before the election: “A president who has made it his business to be a shock to the system retains the capacity to deliver one.”

Even in Australia, which has fought alongside America in every major war since World War I, doubts remain. Dan Ramsay, a University of Sydney politics student, said Wednesday that it would be risky for any country to jump back into relying too heavily on the United States.

“We need to take more seriously our dependencies in a whole bunch of areas and think about how we can maintain an alliance and partnership with the U.S., while also looking elsewhere and strengthening those ties with middle powers around the world,” he said.

Reporting was contributed by Pei-Lin Wu in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, Chris Buckley in Taipei; Keith Bradsher in Beijing, Laura Chung in Sydney, Javier C. Hernández and Kiuko Notoya in Tokyo, Max Kim in Seoul and Pragati K.B. in New Delhi.
